extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, examiners, and policymakers (patent attorneys, biotech/software inventors, USPTO examiners)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether claimed subject matter is patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101 by applying the Supreme Court's judicial-exception framework (e.g., Benson/Flook/Diehr, Bilski, Mayo, Myriad, Alice) and related lower-court interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test (clue, not sole test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The machine-or-transformation test is a useful and important clue, an investigative tool, for determining whether some claimed inventions are processes under § 101, but it is not the sole test for process eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by the Federal Circuit (In re Bilski) as a primary test; Supreme Court in Bilski held it is an important clue but rejected it as the exclusive test. Consider whether a claimed process is tied to a particular machine or transforms an article into a different state as one factor among others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the claim directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea)?
rubrics_metrics.description: First-step inquiry: determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept such as a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court cases (Benson, Flook, Mayo, Alice) begin by identifying whether a claim is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (e.g., Bilski: hedging; Myriad: genetic information). If so, proceed to the second-step inventive-concept inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step Mayo/Alice framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea). Step 2: If so, ask whether the claim contains an ‘inventive concept’ sufficient to ensure the patent amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in Mayo and Alice and implemented by courts and USPTO guidance. Examples: Mayo (diagnostic thresholds held to be law of nature); Alice (intermediated settlement held to be abstract idea). Courts dissect claim elements and evaluate whether additional elements add 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept / 'significantly more' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a judicial exception must contain additional elements (an 'inventive concept') that, individually or as an ordered combination, add significantly more than the ineligible concept itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have examined whether additional steps are merely well-understood, routine, conventional activity (insufficient) or provide something qualitatively different. The opinion criticizes that this inquiry often imports novelty/obviousness-type reasoning (§§102/103) into §101 and can be arbitrary, depending on comparisons to prior §101 opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional activity is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: If the additional steps beyond the judicial exception are well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously engaged in by others in the field, they do not transform an ineligible law of nature or abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayo dissected claim limitations and found that administering, informing, and determining steps amounted to routine activities that add nothing significant. Courts routinely apply this as part of the step-two inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim 'as a whole' vs dissecting into old/new elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Diehr requires that claims be considered as a whole and cautions against dissecting claims into old and new elements and ignoring old elements in the §101 inquiry; Mayo/Flook, by contrast, dissect claim elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diehr: 'a new combination of steps in a process may be patentable even though all the constituents ... were well known' and novelty of elements 'is of no relevance' to §101. The page highlights the conflict between Diehr's whole-claim approach and Mayo/Flook dissection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concern (avoid monopolizing basic tools)
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary concern in judicial exceptions is preventing patents that would preempt broad use of laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas—i.e., monopolization of basic tools of scientific and technological work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts warn against upholding patents that claim processes that too broadly preempt the use of a natural law. This preemption rationale is central to Mayo and other opinions and is used to justify invalidation when claims would monopolize foundational principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior art/state-of-the-art evidence in §101 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have sometimes considered published texts and the state of the art to conclude that a claimed concept is an abstract idea or otherwise ineligible, effectively looking at prior-art-like materials in the §101 inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bilski and Alice relied on existence/ubiquity of known techniques (e.g., hedging, intermediated settlement) and cited texts. The page notes courts did not apply §102 formality (anticipation) but nevertheless used state-of-the-art evidence—raising concerns about importing §§102/103 considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/obviousness should not determine §101 eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelty ('point of novelty') of claim elements and issues properly belonging to §§102 and 103 should not be decisive in determining whether subject matter falls within §101 categories of possibly patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diehr and earlier cases hold that novelty and obviousness are irrelevant to §101; the article criticizes Supreme Court decisions for regressing toward subjective inventiveness and effectively reintroducing these considerations into §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of nature exception (isolated genomic DNA vs cDNA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition that is a product of nature (not made by man) is not patent eligible; the Myriad decision held isolated genomic DNA patent-ineligible while cDNA (created by laboratory processes) was patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad focused on the genetic information encoded in the gene and held that discovery/effort alone insufficiently converts a naturally occurring gene into patentable subject matter. The decision drew a line between isolated genomic DNA and cDNA, though the line is factually and scientifically contentious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered combination notion
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may consider claim limitations collectively as an 'ordered combination' when assessing whether the combination adds significantly more than the judicial exception alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mayo asserted it was sufficient to consider claim limitations as an 'ordered combination' despite Diehr's whole-claim requirement; this has been used to argue that mere aggregation/order of conventional steps can still be insufficient to confer eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental steps / 'pencil-and-paper' test for software-related claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that effectively encompass mental processes or tasks that a person could perform using pen and paper (analyzing information or mathematical algorithms) are treated as abstract ideas and thus potentially ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Synopsys found claims ineligible because the asserted functions could be performed mentally or by hand; the article criticizes this reasoning as potentially sweeping and capable of invalidating many software-implemented inventions.
